summary.text: Specialize to \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and choose an arbitrarily large prime \(p\), for which the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(p\ge e^5\) gives \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the asserted eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\bigl\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime divisor of }k\text{ divides }n\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(\operatorname{PF}(r)\) denotes the set of prime factors of \(r\), then
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in[1,n]:\operatorname{PF}(k)\subseteq \operatorname{PF}(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\in\mathbb N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]

The key observation is that \(a(p)\) is at most \(2\) whenever \(p\) is prime. Indeed, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and every prime factor of \(k\) is also a prime factor of \(p\). If \(k=1\), then \(k\) is one of the two possible values. If \(k>1\), the elementary prime-divisor theorem gives a prime \(q\) dividing \(k\). By the assumed inclusion of prime-factor sets, \(q\) is a prime factor of \(p\), so \(q\mid p\). Since \(p\) is prime, every positive divisor of \(p\) is either \(1\) or \(p\). The number \(q\) is prime and hence is not \(1\), so \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Since \(k>0\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while the defining range already gives \(k\le p\). Therefore \(k=p\). Consequently every integer counted by \(a(p)\) lies in \(\{1,p\}\), and hence
\[
a(p)\le2.
\]
(In fact both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted, so \(a(p)=2\), but only the upper bound is needed.)

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the proposed assertion holds. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There is then some \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a natural number \(m\) with
\[
m>e^5;
\]
such an integer exists by the Archimedean property. Primes are unbounded, so there is a prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
p\ge \max\{N,m\}.
\]
In particular, \(p\ge N\), and therefore the alleged eventual lower bound applies to \(p\). Also
\[
p\ge m>e^5.
\]
Since the logarithm is increasing on the positive real numbers and \(\log(e^5)=5\), it follows that
\[
\log p\ge5.
\]
In particular \(\log p\ge0\).

The asserted lower bound at \(p\), together with the prime-value estimate above, gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)\le2.
\]
Because \(\log p\ge0\), the real one-half power is the nonnegative square root, so
\[
\sqrt{\log p}\le2.
\]
Both sides are nonnegative. Squaring preserves this inequality and yields
\[
\log p=\bigl(\sqrt{\log p}\bigr)^2\le4.
\]
This contradicts \(\log p\ge5\).

Thus the claimed eventual lower bound already fails for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). More concretely, arbitrarily large primes satisfy \(a(p)=2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}\) is unbounded along those primes. Hence it is false that for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has
\[
a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).
